Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: People are not what they seem
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' For a severe mugging-related PTSD profile, markedly fragmented recall and very easy verbal access to the trauma narrative are hard to reconcile as describing the same current memory presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: The Memory node is internally incoherent for a severe mugging/robbery PTSD presentation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' suggests low avoidance and relatively integrated, verbally accessible trauma memory, whereas simultaneously endorsing very vivid detailed recall and body-based painful reliving implies a highly sensory, distressing, poorly integrated trauma memory. This combination is possible in milder cases, but here it is hard to reconcile clinically within the same Memory profile. The Negative Appraisals items are coherent for robbery trauma, but the Memory selections do not fit cleanly with that node pattern or with the strong Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory linkage in the formulation.

issues.item: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: This item is more characteristic of ongoing threat/safety behavior than of a pure negative appraisal. In this profile, Threat is not endorsed and all Threat-related edges are inactive, while the active formulation is specifically centered on a Memory ↔ Negative Appraisals loop. The mistrust items fit robbery-related appraisals, but 'Constant Vigilance' introduces a prominent current-threat theme that is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

vignette: Vikram Patel was thirty-two when he finally stepped into the clinic, his hands still tucked into the pockets of his navy housekeeper’s trousers. It had been nearly two years since the mugging on a rain-slicked service alley behind his apartment building, an event that had quietly reshaped the shape of his days. He remembered the moment with sharp clarity: the sudden grasp at his shoulder, the glint of a blade catching streetlight, the sharp bite of metal against his ribs, and the heavy thud of his own body against wet concrete. He knew what had happened, yet when his wife or his clinic intake coordinator asked him to speak about it, the words would catch in his throat, leaving him nodding rather than answering. What frightened him most was the way the memory returned unfiltered, holding every detail of the alley, the rain, the stranger’s posture, while his body mirrored the old injuries. In the months following the assault, Vikram found himself standing in the hallways of the upscale apartment complexes and corporate offices where he worked, noticing how easily his routine fractured. The memory did not stay in his head; it returned as a physical ache, exactly where the blade had cut. His right ribs tightened, and a dull burn spread across his left forearm whenever he leaned against a doorframe or bent over a laundry cart. He would pause, press a hand to the tender skin, and wait for the sensation to ebb, certain that the streets were no longer places to pass through but spaces to negotiate. He had come to believe that people were not what they seemed, that a smile could easily cover a sudden movement, and he was certain that people simply could not be trusted. The world felt like a dangerous place, and his scores rested at 61, mirroring the quiet persistence of his daily life. This sense of danger and suspicion settled into his daily work. As a housekeeper, Vikram spent his days moving through locked doors and quiet corridors, but he began to notice how the faces of residents and staff held a quiet duplicity. He avoided the main stairwells after six, choosing instead to use the service elevator even when it took longer. When clients or supervisors spoke to him, he kept his answers short and his gaze fixed on the floor or the cleaning caddy beside his feet. His wife, Amara, noticed how he stopped accompanying her to evening walks along the same streets they had once strolled without hesitation. He would wait by the front door, adjusting his cuffs, until the evening grew fully dark and the alleyways seemed too wide, too exposed. The habits accumulated without drama. He stopped carrying his wallet in his front pocket, switching to a secure inner zip that kept the metal wallet against his sternum. He learned to stand with his weight slightly forward, ready to step back if a stranger approached from his right. At work, he began requesting rooms with multiple exits, and when a resident once followed him into a suite to offer a water bottle, Vikram set his cart down and backed toward the doorway, his ribs tight and his breathing shallow. He did not question why his body kept marking the old wounds or why his mind kept cataloguing every face for hidden intent; they simply existed alongside his work, his quiet evenings, and his careful routines. What finally brought Vikram to the clinic was a Tuesday when he was mopping the lobby of his primary residential building. A delivery driver stepped out of the elevator with a parcel, and as their eyes met, Vikram felt the familiar burn across his ribs and the quiet tightening in his throat. He knew the driver meant no harm, but the sensation and the unspoken suspicion arrived together, making the polished lobby feel suddenly narrow. He set the mop against the wall, wiped his palms on his trousers, and called his wife to say he would be stepping out to a professional appointment. He was hoping for a space where he could finally speak the event aloud without losing his words, and where the weight of the danger he carried might be examined, if not entirely set down.
